Defying gravity? Producers stage a musical theatre revival | Stage

There’s a worldwide trend in musical theatre that bigger must be better. Melbourne’s spectacular, yet theatrically unremarkable King Kong is the perfect example. Not only does the star of the show stand a massive six metres tall, but the budget reportedly tops $30 million. But have Australia’s musical giants been keeping the little guys out of the room for too long?

New York has long had a healthy Off-Broadway musical theatre scene where smaller and riskier works flourish. Some shows break through, connect with an audience and make it to the big time. But despite a few success stories, such as Belvoir's political comedy Keating! which started out at Melbourne International Comedy Festival and went on to tour for three years, Australia has never really had a culture of supporting experimentation in musical theatre, and the industry has suffered because of it.

A group of musical theatre producers on Tuesday announced their plan to inject new life into local musical theatre. Having won the bid to run an 111-seat theatre at Potts Point in Sydney for three years – the Darlinghurst Theatre Company is moving to a new venue – they plan to make it the home of musical theatre in the city, working together under the banner of Independent Music Theatre (IMT).

They hope to bring intimate musical theatre back to Sydney, producing new local and international musicals alongside reimagined classics and cabarets. For a city that hasn't had a smaller professional venue devoted purely to musical theatre in decades – while there are a few similar venues around Australia, none that I know of are professional – that's an important addition. Not least because of the calibre of the producers involved.

They include Neil Gooding, who has produced theatre across Australia and most recently was a producer for Alan Cumming’s one man Macbeth on Broadway. He’s also produced local works including original Australian musical the Hatpin, which went on to have a successful season at the New York Musical Theatre Festival.

Gooding believes there’s a real hunger for the intimate musical experience in Australia, but producers have struggled without a dedicated venue. “I think there has been quite a lot of quality small musical theatre and cabaret programming,” he says. “But it’s been a difficult process to let the audience know where that programming is happening because if you keep dispersing yourself over three or four different venues, they never know really know where they’re seeing it, who’s producing it or what the quality will be.”

Also involved is Squabbalogic, a company that this year is producing Off-Broadway hit Bloody Bloody Andrew Jackson, Luckiest productions, whose team include David and Lisa Campbell who were behind the Adelaide Cabaret Festival for several years, and Neglected Musicals .

They will have some work to do to convince Australia's “serious” theatregoers that musical theatre is worth engaging with. Which is unsurprising when the current attitude seems to be that a musical without a cast of 20 and a multi-million dollar set isn't really a musical. With most shows arriving from overseas – their sensational sets and costumes pre-packed and ready to perform – musicals have long been seen as a purely commercial venture in Australia; the domain of producers who can put in the big bucks in the hope of getting a good return.

The intimate musical theatre experience is something altogether different. It throws the focus back onto the performers, direction and writing and allows an audience to connect with the subtleties of a work. In a theatre that holds only 111, there really is nowhere to hide.

David Campbell, producer with Luckiest productions, believes IMT can coexist with the bigger shows and is just another side of the musical theatre coin. “Having something like this works hand in hand with the big shows that come through town and provides more affordable content. One of our inspirations was the Menier Chocolate Factory model and the Roundabout and the Donmar Warehouse. You can do established musicals, new musicals and cabaret,” he says.

While IMT is still very much in the early stages and Campbell isn’t prepared to talk finances, the organisation is not-for-profit and won’t have Cameron Mackintosh’s $10m plus budget – which will be reflected in ticket prices. Time will tell if they can live up to their mission of becoming a home for music theatre, supporting new talent and new work, but the intention and the know-how is definitely there.

Independent Music Theatre to take over Darlinghurst Theatre Venue

Potts Point will be the home for music theatre and cabaret in Sydney when Independent Music Theatre (IMT) take over the stage of the Reginald Murphy Hall currently known as the Darlinghurst Theatre.

Independent Music Theatre, a not-for-profit company made up of an artistic group of cabaret and music theatre specialists, has been awarded the tender from City of Sydney Council to take over the venue.

Independent Music Theatre is a collaborative partnership between organisations that currently present or facilitate music theatre, cabaret and small-scale musicals in Sydney and across Australia.

The artistic group includes Luckiest Productions: David Campbell, Lisa Campbell and Richard Carroll; Neglected Musicals: Michelle Guthrie; Squabbalogic: Jay James-Moody and Jessica Burns; Neil Gooding Productions: Neil Gooding; and independent producers Michael Huxley and Simone Parrott.

“We are creating a home for music theatre and cabaret,” said Neil Gooding, IMT Company Director.

“This will allow writers, directors, musical directors, choreographers, performers and designers to develop not only new work but also specifically tailored small scale musical theatre from Australia, Broadway and The West End.”

The collaborative partnership will seek to provide a cultural hub where artists can share resources and knowledge, nurturing their skills though exploration, creation, presentation and audience development of theatrical works.

“We will present a range of performances including new musicals, re-imagined classics, small scale new work from Australia and overseas, cabaret, children’s productions and connect with an already established audience,” said David Campbell.

“This intimate venue gives audiences the opportunity to enjoy an up close and personal style of music theatre.”

In the coming weeks Independent Music Theatre will announce a renaming of the venue and plans for the future.

For more information, visit: www.independentmusictheatre.com for details.
